title: Past Tense or Present Perfect?
goal: Choose between past tense and present perfect when talking about specific past events, experiences, results, unfinished periods, duration, and narrative sequences.

objectives.statement: Choose between past tense and present perfect when talking about specific past events, experiences, results, unfinished periods, duration, and narrative sequences.

spans.value: Leila and Jonas work in the same office. They are deciding whether to get something to eat after work.
Har du vært på Fjordhuset før?

blocks.translation: Have you been to Fjordhuset before?

spans.value: Ja, jeg var der forrige fredag. Først spiste vi middag, og så hørte vi på et band.

blocks.translation: Yes, I was there last Friday. First we had dinner, and then we listened to a band.

spans.value: Jeg har aldri spist der, men jeg har hørt mye positivt om stedet.

blocks.translation: I have never eaten there, but I have heard many positive things about the place.

spans.value: Skal vi gå dit nå, da?

blocks.translation: Shall we go there now, then?

spans.value: Gjerne, men jeg har allerede spist. Jeg kan ta en kaffe.

blocks.translation: Sure, but I have already eaten. I can have a coffee.

spans.value: Du spiste tidlig!
Ja. Jeg har jobbet siden klokka åtte i dag, så jeg tok lunsj før elleve.

blocks.translation: Yes. I have worked since eight o’clock today, so I had lunch before eleven.

spans.value: Jeg har bodd i dette området i tre år, men jeg finner fortsatt nye steder.

blocks.translation: I have lived in this area for three years, but I still find new places.

spans.value: Jeg bodde i Bergen i tre år før jeg flyttet hit. Der gikk jeg ofte på små konserter.

blocks.translation: I lived in Bergen for three years before I moved here. There I often went to small concerts.

spans.value: Both speakers are talking about the past, but they do not always use the same tense. Sometimes they place an event inside a completed past time: last Friday, before eleven, or before a move. At other times, they connect the past with the present: an experience at some time before now, a meal whose result matters now, or a situation that began earlier and continues.
This chapter contrasts the
past tense (preteritum)
with the
present perfect (presens perfektum)
. You already know how these forms are made. The focus here is choosing between them.
Compare:

no.value: Jeg var på Fjordhuset forrige fredag.

en.value: I was at Fjordhuset last Friday.

no.value: Jeg har vært på Fjordhuset før.

en.value: I have been to Fjordhuset before.

spans.value: The past tense places the visit in a completed past time:
forrige fredag
. The present perfect presents it as part of Leila’s experience before now. It does not say when the visit happened.
A useful first rule is:

items.value: Use the past tense when the event belongs to a specific, completed past time.
Use the present perfect when the past event is connected to now and no completed past time is being stated.

spans.value: This is a meaning choice, not merely a choice between two verb forms.
The past tense is the normal choice when you say when a completed event happened.

no.value: Jeg besøkte Tromsø i fjor.

en.value: I visited Tromsø last year.

no.value: Hun kjøpte bilen i mandags.

en.value: She bought the car last Monday.

no.value: Vi så filmen i går kveld.

en.value: We watched the film yesterday evening.

no.value: De flyttet hit i 2022.

en.value: They moved here in 2022.

spans.value: Expressions such as
i går
yesterday
forrige uke
last week
i mandags
last Monday
), and
identify completed past times.
The same principle applies when a question asks for a specific past occasion:

no.value: Når kjøpte du bilen?

en.value: When did you buy the car?

no.value: Hvor bodde dere i fjor?

en.value: Where did you live last year?

spans.value: A common mistake is to combine the present perfect with an explicitly completed past time:

no.value: ✗ Jeg har sett filmen i går.

en.value: Intended meaning: I watched the film yesterday.

spans.value: Because
i går
is finished, Norwegian normally requires:

no.value: Jeg så filmen i går.

en.value: I watched the film yesterday.

spans.value: The problem is not that the film has no relevance now. The problem is that the speaker has placed the event inside a completed past time.
Use the present perfect to ask or say whether something has happened at any time before now when the exact occasion is not important.

no.value: Har du vært i Tromsø?

en.value: Have you been to Tromsø?

no.value: Jeg har aldri reist alene.

en.value: I have never travelled alone.

no.value: Hun har sett den filmen tre ganger.

en.value: She has seen that film three times.

no.value: Vi har prøvd den nye restauranten.

en.value: We have tried the new restaurant.

spans.value: These sentences describe experience accumulated up to the present. Words such as
før
before
aldri
never
noen gang
ever
), and
tre ganger
three times
) often appear in this use.
Compare the questions:

no.value: Har du noen gang kjørt til Bergen?

en.value: Have you ever driven to Bergen?

no.value: Kjørte du til Bergen i fjor sommer?

en.value: Did you drive to Bergen last summer?

spans.value: The first asks about experience at any time before now. The second asks about one completed period.
In a fuller answer, Leila could combine both: «Ja, jeg har vært på Fjordhuset før. Jeg var der forrige fredag.»

no.value: Ja, jeg har vært på Fjordhuset før.

en.value: Yes, I have been to Fjordhuset before.

no.value: Jeg var der forrige fredag.

en.value: I was there last Friday.

spans.value: The first sentence establishes the experience. The second identifies a particular visit.
Present perfect can also emphasize a present result. The event happened earlier, but its consequence explains the current situation.
In the dialogue, Jonas says:

no.value: Jeg har allerede spist.

en.value: I have already eaten.

spans.value: His meal matters because Leila has suggested getting food now. He is not telling the story of when he ate; he is explaining his present state.
Compare:

no.value: Jeg har mistet nøklene.

en.value: I have lost the keys.

spans.value: This normally suggests that the keys are still missing or that the loss is a current problem.

no.value: Jeg mistet nøklene på bussen i går.

en.value: I lost the keys on the bus yesterday.

spans.value: This places the loss in a completed past setting and reports what happened.
Another useful contrast:

no.value: Har du gjort leksene?

en.value: Have you done the homework?

spans.value: The question asks whether the homework is complete now.

no.value: Gjorde du leksene etter skolen?

en.value: Did you do the homework after school?

spans.value: The question asks what happened during a particular past period.
Present perfect does not automatically mean “recent.” A recent event can still take the past tense if the speaker locates it at a finished time:

no.value: Jeg sendte meldingen klokka tre.

en.value: I sent the message at three o’clock.

spans.value: Conversely, an older event can use present perfect if it is presented as relevant experience:

no.value: Jeg har lest den boka flere ganger.

en.value: I have read that book several times.

spans.value: Some time expressions can refer to a period that is still continuing. In that case, present perfect often reports what has happened within the period up to now.

no.value: Jeg har lest to kapitler i dag.

en.value: I have read two chapters today.

no.value: Vi har hatt tre møter denne uka.

en.value: We have had three meetings this week.

no.value: Hun har ringt meg flere ganger i år.

en.value: She has called me several times this year.

spans.value: Here,
i dag
denne uka
, and
i år
are viewed as unfinished periods. The speaker is taking stock of events up to the present.
Compare them with completed periods:

no.value: Jeg leste to kapitler i går.

en.value: I read two chapters yesterday.

no.value: Vi hadde tre møter forrige uke.

en.value: We had three meetings last week.

no.value: Hun ringte meg flere ganger i fjor.

en.value: She called me several times last year.

spans.value: A period can be unfinished while one event inside it is located at a specific completed point:

no.value: Jeg har jobbet mye i dag.

en.value: I have worked a lot today.

no.value: Jeg snakket med sjefen klokka ni i dag.

en.value: I spoke with the manager at nine today.

spans.value: The first sentence summarizes the day up to now. The second places one completed conversation at nine o’clock. Therefore,
i dag
does not mechanically force present perfect. The speaker’s viewpoint still matters.
Duration creates a particularly important contrast.

no.value: Jeg har bodd i dette området i tre år.

en.value: I have lived in this area for three years.

spans.value: This means that Leila moved there three years ago and still lives there.

no.value: Jeg bodde i Bergen i tre år.

en.value: I lived in Bergen for three years.

spans.value: This presents the period of living in Bergen as finished. Jonas no longer lives there.
More contrasts:

no.value: Hun har jobbet her siden 2021.

en.value: She has worked here since 2021.

spans.value: She still works here.

no.value: Hun jobbet der fra 2021 til 2024.

en.value: She worked there from 2021 to 2024.

spans.value: That job belongs to a finished period.

no.value: Vi har ventet i en time.

en.value: We have waited for an hour.

spans.value: The waiting began an hour ago and is still relevant, usually because it is continuing now.

no.value: Vi ventet i en time før bussen kom.

en.value: We waited for an hour before the bus came.

spans.value: The arrival of the bus completed the waiting period.
Time expressions with
siden
since
) naturally point from a starting point to now when the situation continues:

no.value: Jeg har kjent Nora siden videregående.

en.value: I have known Nora since secondary school.

spans.value: An expression with
i
plus a duration can occur with either tense. The tense tells you whether the situation continues:

no.value: Han har studert norsk i to år.

en.value: He has studied Norwegian for two years.

spans.value: He is still studying it.

no.value: Han studerte norsk i to år.

en.value: He studied Norwegian for two years.

spans.value: That period is presented as finished.
When you narrate a sequence of completed events, the past tense moves the story forward.
Her visit, told as a full sequence:

no.value: Først spiste vi middag. Så hørte vi på et band. Etterpå tok vi bussen hjem.

en.value: First we had dinner. Then we listened to a band. Afterwards we took the bus home.

spans.value: All three actions form a completed sequence. Present perfect would not normally be used for each step in this kind of narrative.
A speaker can begin with present perfect to establish relevance and then switch to past tense for details:

no.value: Jeg har vært på Fjordhuset én gang. Jeg dro dit med kollegaene mine. Vi spiste middag, hørte på musikk og gikk hjem ved midnatt.

en.value: I have been to Fjordhuset once. I went there with my colleagues. We had dinner, listened to music, and went home at midnight.

spans.value: The first sentence answers an experience question. The following sentences tell the story of that particular occasion.
Compare:

no.value: Det har skjedd noe på kontoret.

en.value: Something has happened at the office.

spans.value: This introduces a current situation.

no.value: Først sluttet internettet å virke. Så ringte vi IT-avdelingen. Til slutt startet vi alle maskinene på nytt.

en.value: First the internet stopped working. Then we called the IT department. Finally we restarted all the computers.

spans.value: The details form a completed narrative sequence, so they use the past tense.
Jonas’s tense choices reveal what kind of information he is giving.

no.value: Jeg har allerede spist.

en.value: I have already eaten.

spans.value: This explains why he does not need dinner now.

no.value: Jeg har jobbet siden klokka åtte i dag.

en.value: I have worked since eight o’clock today.

spans.value: His working period began earlier and continues up to the present context.

no.value: Jeg tok lunsj før elleve.

en.value: I had lunch before eleven.

spans.value: This meal is placed at a completed past time.

no.value: Jeg bodde i Bergen i tre år før jeg flyttet hit.

en.value: I lived in Bergen for three years before I moved here.

spans.value: Both living in Bergen and moving away belong to a finished past sequence.
Leila also moves naturally between the two tenses:

no.value: Jeg har bodd i dette området i tre år.

en.value: I have lived in this area for three years.

spans.value: She still lives there.

no.value: Jeg var på Fjordhuset forrige fredag.

en.value: I was at Fjordhuset last Friday.

spans.value: Her visit happened during a completed past period.
Before choosing a tense, ask what the listener needs to understand.
Use the
past tense (preteritum)
when:

items.value: the event occurred at a specific completed past time;
the sentence advances a completed narrative sequence.

spans.value: Use the
present perfect (presens perfektum)
when:

items.value: the sentence describes experience before now without saying when;
an earlier event has a result that matters now;
events are counted or summarized within an unfinished period;
a state or activity began earlier and continues now.

spans.value: Do not decide from “recent” versus “long ago.” Decide whether the speaker places the event in a finished past frame or connects it to the present.

Imagine that Sara is preparing for guests tonight. She began cleaning this morning and is still working. She wants to report what is ready now, mention something she did at a specific time, describe how long she has lived in the flat, and tell the sequence of events from a dinner she hosted last month.

prompt.value: Classify what motivates each highlighted verb in Leila and Jonas’s dialogue. Use the stated time expression, sequence, experience, present consequence, or continuing situation—not verb form alone.

explanation.value: Use preterite with a finished, specified past time; use present perfect for experience, present relevance, or a period continuing to now.

Du spiste tidlig! (A completed meal earlier today.)
Jeg har jobbet siden klokka åtte i dag. (The working period continues.)
Jeg har bodd i dette området i tre år. (Leila still lives there.)
Jeg bodde i Bergen i tre år før jeg flyttet hit.
Jeg bodde i Bergen før jeg flyttet hit.
Da jeg bodde i Bergen, gikk jeg ofte på små konserter.

prompt.value: Build the complete account. Begin with experience before now, then use past tense throughout the particular completed evening.

tokens.text: Forrige fredag dro jeg dit med kollegaene mine.
Jeg har vært på Fjordhuset én gang.

prompt.value: Write Leila’s connected Norwegian message to a colleague. State that she has been to Fjordhuset before, that she was there last Friday, and what she did there. Explain that Jonas only wants coffee tonight because he has already eaten. Also state that Leila has lived in the area for three years and still lives there. Use appropriate past tense or present perfect for every relationship.

payload.judge_prompt: Check the message against each requested meaning. Accept natural Bokmål wording and word-order variants when tense and time relationship remain clear. Report evidence for every criterion.

criteria.instruction: Uses present perfect to state Leila’s prior experience with Fjordhuset.
Uses past tense for Leila’s visit last Friday.
Uses past tense for what Leila did during that completed visit.
Uses present perfect to explain that Jonas only wants coffee because he has already eaten.
Uses present perfect to state that Leila has lived in the area for three years and still lives there.
Presents the requested meanings as one understandable connected message.

prompt.value: Write one coherent Norwegian paragraph about Sara. She is still cleaning for guests tonight and has cleaned a lot today. The food is ready now because she has made dinner. She sent a message at three o’clock. She has lived in the flat for four years and still lives there. She has hosted guests before. Last month she hosted a completed dinner: first the guests arrived, then they ate, and afterwards they went home. Express all six time relationships with appropriate tenses.

payload.judge_prompt: Check whether the paragraph expresses every supplied situation with the tense required by its viewpoint. Accept natural Bokmål variants that preserve all meanings. Report evidence for each criterion.

criteria.instruction: Uses present perfect to summarize Sara’s cleaning within today, which is still continuing.
Uses present perfect for making dinner when its present result is that the food is ready.
Uses past tense for sending a message at three o’clock.
Uses present perfect for living in the flat for four years when Sara still lives there.
Uses present perfect to state that Sara has hosted guests before.
Uses past tense consistently for the arrival, meal, and departure during last month’s completed dinner.
Integrates all requested meanings into one understandable paragraph.

prompt.value: Write five controlled Norwegian examples: one sentence about an unspecified experience, one about an event yesterday, one about a result that matters now, one about an activity continuing since a stated starting point, and one containing two completed events in sequence. Keep all five examples in Norwegian and make each time meaning clear.

payload.judge_prompt: Check each Norwegian example against its assigned meaning. Accept varied natural Bokmål vocabulary when tense and time reference agree. Report evidence for every criterion.

criteria.instruction: Uses present perfect to give a natural Norwegian sentence about an unspecified experience before now.
Uses past tense for a natural Norwegian sentence about an event yesterday.
Uses present perfect for a natural Norwegian sentence about a result that matters now.
Uses present perfect for a natural Norwegian sentence about an activity continuing since a stated starting point.
Uses past tense for a natural Norwegian sentence containing two completed events in sequence.
